The currency of most former French colonies in West and Central Africa, created by France in 1945. There are in fact two CFA francs, one for eight West African states and one for six in Central Africa, each with its own central bank. They are used across the old French West Africa and French Equatorial Africa.

The franc was pegged to the French franc, and since 1999 to the euro, at a fixed rate. France guaranteed that it could be exchanged, and in return the member states had to keep a large share of their foreign reserves at the French Treasury.

Supporters say the system kept inflation low and gave stability. Critics, many of them African economists, call it a leftover of colonial rule that ties monetary policy to Paris. In 1994 France forced a devaluation that cut the currency's value in half overnight. In 2019 the West African states and France agreed to reforms: the reserve rule ended, and France left the governing boards, with plans for a new West African currency, the eco, linked to the work of ECOWAS.
